harness: Each row's example runs in this harness: `container` is the timeline's element, `items` five items over March 2026 in two lanes (`lanes`), `DAY` a day in milliseconds. `before` runs before `createTimeline`, `config` goes into its configuration, `after` runs with `timeline`. In React, the configuration is the props of `<Timeline>` from `@temporeum/timeline-react`. Every plugin is registered first (`registerPlugin` with the Gantt chart, the resource view, export, the time tools, groups, item kinds and other languages), as a page moving from react-calendar-timeline would: react-calendar-timeline draws all of its features without asking. Register only the ones your configuration uses, and a page loads only those.

statuses.renamed: Same meaning, another name or place.
statuses.different: Possible, done another way — read the note.

rows.note: In React the same configuration is `<Timeline items={items} lanes={lanes} domain={domain} />` from `@temporeum/timeline-react`; every key on this page is the same prop, and each event `x` is an `onX` prop.

rows.vis: moment or dayjs as a peer dependency
rows.note: No date library. A moment or a dayjs converts with `.valueOf()`.
rows.before:
const fromLibrary = { valueOf: () => Date.UTC(2026, 2, 12) };
const meeting = { id: "meeting", laneId: "work", label: "Meeting", start: fromLibrary.valueOf() };

rows.note: Ids are strings.
rows.before:
const rctGroups = [{ id: 3, title: "Support" }];
const moreLanes = rctGroups.map((group) => ({ id: String(group.id), label: group.title }));

rows.vis: items: [{ id, group, title, start_time, end_time }]
rows.note: Ids are strings; `group` is `laneId`; times are a `Date` or epoch milliseconds.
rows.before:
const rctItem = { id: 9, group: "ship", title: "Hotfix", start_time: Date.UTC(2026, 2, 16), end_time: Date.UTC(2026, 2, 18) };
const hotfix = { id: String(rctItem.id), laneId: String(rctItem.group), label: rctItem.title, start: rctItem.start_time, end: rctItem.end_time };

rows.note: There is one shape for items and lanes; convert other field names when the data comes in.
rows.before:
const raw = [{ uid: "x1", name: "Renamed fields", from: Date.UTC(2026, 2, 24), lane: "work" }];
const mapped = raw.map((each) => ({ id: each.uid, label: each.name, start: each.from, laneId: each.lane }));

rows.note: The timeline follows its container's size; below `breakpoint` it turns vertical when `orientation` is `"auto"`.
The container is the host's element; style it, and the theme's custom properties.
Without a domain the view fits the items, with a margin.
The timeline owns its view: set it with `zoomTo`, hear about it with `viewportChanged`. In React, take the instance with `timelineRef`.
rows.after:
timeline.on("viewportChanged", ({ viewport }) => console.log(viewport.domain));
timeline.zoomTo([new Date("2026-03-05"), new Date("2026-03-20")]);

rows.note: The shortest and longest visible span, in milliseconds, as in react-calendar-timeline.
Nothing to set: once touched, the view draws a viewport ahead on each side while it rests.
A plain wheel scrolls or pans; ctrl + wheel and a pinch zoom; `+` and `-` zoom from the keyboard. `interactions.zoom: false` turns zooming off.
The lane labels head their rows; with `laneHeaders` they stay in view while the view pans.
Row height follows the density; `auto` picks one at which every row fits.
The least size across, in CSS pixels; a lane grows with its rows.
react-calendar-timeline overlaps items unless told to stack; Temporeum packs them into rows unless told otherwise. `packMode: "overlap"` is react-calendar-timeline's default.
A `template` is sanitised HTML in place of the label; `hooks.renderItem` returns scene nodes, and also renders on the server.
One function for every axis label; `tick.granularity` says what it stands for.
The library never reads the clock; the host passes the time, and updates it if it should move.

rows.temporeum: decorations: [{ kind: "marker", id, time }], or timeBars
rows.note: A marker is drawn; a time bar (`timeBars`) can also be dragged, and says so with `timeBarMoved`.
rows.config: decorations: [{ kind: "marker", id: "freeze", time: new Date("2026-03-25"), label: "Code freeze" }]

rows.note: react-calendar-timeline is editable until told otherwise; Temporeum is read-only until `editing.enabled`. Moving between lanes is `crossLane`.

rows.after: timeline.updateItems([{ id: "design", movable: false, resizable: false }]);

rows.note: In milliseconds, as in react-calendar-timeline, from the epoch or `snapOrigin`.
A least duration in time, not a least width in pixels.
Return `false` to refuse the move or the resize; snapping is `snapMs`.
rows.config: editing: { enabled: true, canMove: (item, next) => item.id !== "launch" || next.laneId === undefined }

rows.note: A double tap on empty lane space, or `n`, adds an item; `createItem` says what it is.
Also fires for `Enter` on the focused item.
One event with the ids now selected and before.
Carries the item, where it was and where it is (`to.start`, `to.laneId`), and the reversible command. The library never saves.
rows.after: timeline.on("itemMoved", ({ item, to }) => console.log(item.id, to.start, to.laneId));
timeline.on("itemResized", ({ item, to }) => console.log(item.id, to.start, to.end));

rows.note: With its `reason`: `zoom`, `pan`, `resize`, `api`.
A drag on empty time selects a range; a click on it selects nothing.
A move is reported once, when it ends (`itemMoved`); `getSnapshot().editing` says one is under way.
Listen for `contextmenu` on the container.
An item is resized at its edges, or with `Shift` and an arrow.
One column of lane labels.
Lane labels are text.
Ticks are chosen for the zoom level; `formatTick` writes them.
`decorations: [{ kind: "banding" }]` alternates the tick bands; a class per time is not supported.
Groups take a `className` (`groups`); plain lanes do not.
Use `className` and a stylesheet.
The axis is one band, drawn by the library; `formatTick` writes its labels.
The view moves with `zoomTo` and `scrollTo`, not a scroll element.
